about.title: About
about.paragraph:
Hello, I'm Abdelrahman Ameen.

I love technology, games, and making things. I've been working in software development and interactive media for over five years, working on games, software, graphics, tools, simulation, visualization, and plenty of things in between.

I'm fascinated by games as a medium. I love how playing a game can connect you with an idea, a story, a place, or an experience in a way few other mediums can. Games can also bring people together and help us share ideas and cultures across different backgrounds.

That's a big part of why I make games. I'm always curious about what makes a game work, why something is fun, how a mechanic communicates with the player, and how design and technology come together to create an experience.

Over the years, I've worked across different parts of development, from Unreal Engine and custom graphics systems to game mechanics, tools, software, and interactive projects.

There's a bit of this and that in this portfolio.

Have a look around.

projects.title: Project Ultra
projects.shortDescription: Sci-fi third-person shooter I made alone in Unreal. Multiplayer, Epic Online Services, alpha on itch.
projects.fullDescription:
I built Project Ultra by myself in Unreal Engine. Sci-fi, third person, and the alpha lives on itch.io.

Matchmaking, login, and player data go through Epic Online Services.

Movement, combat, weapons, the session UI, and the networking are all in there. I was the whole team, so the game and the online layer had to ship together.

projects.title: Back to Back
projects.shortDescription: Asymmetric co-op on Steam. Two players, three periods of Egypt, Unreal Engine 5.5.
projects.fullDescription:
Back to Back shipped on Steam. Unreal Engine 5.5. Two people play through three historical periods of Egypt, each with its own spaces, roles, and trouble.

Abilities are split across the two players. Matchmaking is Steam.

I worked on enemy AI for ranged, melee, and special types, including pathfinding and how they choose to fight, even as a squad. Bosses run in phases with readable attacks, and difficulty moves with how you're doing. Traps are modular: spot them, disarm them. Weapons can be customized, upgraded, and comboed.

AI authoring used Behavior Trees and EQS. Traps and weapons are custom gameplay code. Online play uses the Steam SDK.

projects.title: Time Bomb
projects.shortDescription: Small Unreal 5.5 side-scroller about time. Proof of concept. One level.
projects.fullDescription:
I made Time Bomb in Unreal Engine 5.5 to try one idea: controlling time. 3D side-scroller. You climb out of a lab across a single authored level.

Pause time to thread jumps and hazards. Rewind to put terrain back or move relative to enemies. Pickups add a double jump and a longer rewind, and you can bounce projectiles and change walkways while the clock is doing whatever you told it to.

Blueprints drive the level. The main menu uses a MetaHuman. The level is supposed to teach the system by playing it, so I left out a separate tutorial screen.

projects.title: Duck, Duck... BOOM!
projects.shortDescription: Cartoon 3D top-down shooter, still in development. I was a technical game designer. Time is the resource. Hits and abilities take seconds off your life.
projects.fullDescription:
Duck, Duck... BOOM! is a 3D cartoon singleplayer top-down shooter. I was a technical game designer on it, listed under Design on the itch.io page.

Ducks showed up. They swarm. They don't talk it out, and there's a bomb in the middle of that mess.

Health bars and ammo counters are gone. Time is what you have. A hit steals seconds. A dash through duck fire costs time, and an overcharged shotgun costs more. You last, or you spend lifespan to push through.

Still in development. Keyboard, mouse, and gamepad. Action, 3D, cartoon, singleplayer. No generative AI.

Dev team from itch.io: Design is Bassel Mostafa (Bassel Kamel) and Abdelrahman Ameen. Art is Sarah Alaa and Mariam Ayman. Tech is Ali Abdat and Amr Hamed.

Asset credits from itch.io: Defender: Top-Down Shooter v3.3, Chameleon Post Process, Hero for RPG : Modular Polyart, POLYGON - Town Pack, and Cute Cartoon Boy With Cloth on Fab. Music from Uppbeat.

projects.title: Justice Seeker: Unsafe Data
projects.shortDescription: Fully voiced detective game from Jana Games. TBA on Steam. I came on as a freelance developer.
projects.fullDescription:
Justice Seeker: Unsafe Data is Jana Games' detective narrative game. Fully voiced. I worked on it freelance.

You're Axel Zakon, ex-police, now private. The police pull you into a homicide and won't say why. The victim is the CEO of TechDB, a big data company in the city. You look for clues, work the rooms, and talk to people.

The Steam page calls it a dark story with twists, including whatever ties you to the victim, plus a cast that sets the tone, free movement through TechDB floor by floor (go back later and new things can show up), close-up inspection, photos, interrogations, and getting someone arrested.

Jana Games is developer and publisher. Release is to be announced. Adventure, indie, RPG, strategy. Single-player. English UI, full audio, subtitles. Award: Best Graphics - GCCDZ. Mature: mild gore and blood.

projects.title: SFML Pac-Man
projects.shortDescription: Pac-Man in C++ and SFML. I spent most of the time on ghost AI and the old movement rules.
projects.fullDescription:
I rebuilt Pac-Man in C++ with SFML because I wanted the ghosts and the original movement rules to feel right.

Ghosts switch states and path the way the arcade game does. Maze collision, sprites, and audio go through SFML, kept light enough for that kind of real-time loop.

I made it to sit with classic game AI in C++, close to the metal, with no engine doing the thinking.

projects.title: TASM-Space-Invaders
projects.shortDescription: Space Invaders in x86 assembly (TASM). Drawing, timing, and sound go straight at the hardware.
projects.fullDescription:
Space Invaders in x86 assembly with TASM. Rendering, timing, collision, and audio sit next to the hardware on purpose.

Sprites go into video memory. Timing is interrupt-driven so the frame pacing stays honest. Enemy motion and hits are assembly. Feedback is the PC speaker.

I wanted a game loop I could see. Memory layout, interrupts, nothing sitting between me and the machine.

projects.title: Organito (Graduation Project)
projects.shortDescription: Medical visualization for students. Graduation project, team of four. I wrote the C++ renderer: DICOM volume ray marching, HU tissue windows, marching-cubes meshes, compiled to WASM with Emscripten for a Tauri app on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
projects.fullDescription:
Organito is a medical visualization app for students. Graduation project. Four of us. One person on deployment with Kubernetes and Docker, one on the software-engineering side of the app, and I was mostly rendering and visualization.

Desktop app for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Tauri on the outside, Rust on the backend, and a C++ rendering library I wrote so we could compile the same engine to WebAssembly with Emscripten and some JavaScript glue.

The library is C++17 on OpenGL ES 3.0 / WebGL 2. It ray-marches volumetric CT data and can export marching-cubes meshes. In the Tauri app I wrote the JavaScript that loads the WASM module, owns the canvas, and drives those systems.

DICOM slices get parsed on the host (rows, columns, pixels, RescaleSlope, RescaleIntercept), converted to Hounsfield units, sorted by slice location, and uploaded as an R32F 3D texture. The C++ side does not copy that volume through the WASM heap. JavaScript creates the texture on the shared WebGL 2 context, and each frame a JS callback binds it before the volume pass. A full-screen fragment shader builds a camera ray, hits the volume box, and marches with trilinear sampling. HU maps to density, then a window isolates a tissue range (skin, soft tissue, organs, bone) and the rest drops out. Opacity is a transfer function, gradients shade the surface, and samples composite front-to-back with an early out. The same HU windows feed mesh generation. We 3D-printed soft tissue and hard tissue as separate prints.

I also put SDF ray marching in the library, and sped up the visualization path with SDFs and BVHs.

My code is in the Raymarching repo. renderer is the C++ library: headers, implementation, Emscripten bindings, WASM build. Monorepo - Copy is a copy of the full app, Tauri host included, plus the viewer that loads DICOM, picks tissue presets, and calls into the WASM module.

projects.title: Custom 3D Game Engine
projects.shortDescription: C++20 OpenGL engine I built for a third-person beat 'em up prototype. Physics, animation, rendering, audio.
projects.fullDescription:
A 3D engine in C++20 and OpenGL for a third-person beat 'em up prototype. Physics, skeletal animation, rendering, audio, and gameplay sit in an ECS.

Physics is ReactPhysics3D: rigid bodies, dynamic/static/kinematic, a few collider types, debug draw in the main view.

Rendering is a forward OpenGL path with a cubemap skybox, directional/point/spot lights, transparency, post-process, and materials with diffuse, specular, and normal maps. Models come in through Assimp (OBJ, DAE). Skeletal animation walks a bone hierarchy and interpolates keyframes.

Audio is OpenAL, positional. Scenes save and load as JSON.

In the prototype you can swap the playable character, fight, collect things, and there's enemy AI. Debug views for colliders and engine internals.

Stack: C++20, OpenGL, GLFW, ReactPhysics3D, Assimp, OpenAL, JSON for Modern C++.

projects.title: Vulkan Ray Tracing Engine with Monte Carlo Integration
projects.shortDescription: Vulkan ray tracing, Monte Carlo, importance sampling. I wanted global illumination, soft shadows, and reflections on RTX hardware.
projects.fullDescription:
Real-time physically based renderer on Vulkan's ray tracing extensions. Monte Carlo integration and cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling. I was aiming at global illumination, soft shadows, reflections, and indirect light, with RTX doing the acceleration.

Vulkan 1.3, VK_KHR_ray_tracing_pipeline and VK_KHR_acceleration_structure. Shaders are GLSL to SPIR-V. GLM for the math. I tested on NVIDIA RTX cards, 3060 and up.

I wanted to approximate the rendering equation by integrating, pick up indirect light and caustics, and compare a CPU path with the GPU one. I also looked at how noise and error change with the sample budget.

BLAS/TLAS BVHs, ray-gen / closest-hit / miss, multi-bounce transport with unbiased Monte Carlo, importance sampling to cut variance.

On RTX hardware it does real-time HD. More than 1,000 samples per pixel in under a second. The Python reference was about one sample per second. More samples and the cosine-weighted hemisphere make the noise less ugly.

projects.title: Vulkan Abstraction Engine
projects.shortDescription: C++20 wrapper over Vulkan. RAII and a type-safer API. Vulkan stays visible.
projects.fullDescription:
A C++20 layer on top of Vulkan. I wanted something less painful to call, and I still wanted to see what the GPU was doing.

Resources are RAII. The API is typed with C++20. Errors and memory stay explicit. It runs across platforms.

Smart pointers and templates around resource lifetime, plus abstractions for command buffers, pipelines, descriptors, and sync, and memory pools for allocations so pipeline state and descriptor sets stay things you think about without the usual noise.

Less boilerplate. Lifetimes you can still see. Performance that stays close to writing Vulkan by hand.

projects.title: AstraTrace
projects.shortDescription: C++20 CPU path tracer for glTF 2.0. Whitted ray tracing, progressive path tracing, textured PBR, SDL/ImGui viewer. CPU only.
projects.fullDescription:
AstraTrace is a C++20 physically based software renderer for glTF 2.0. Path tracer. CPU only. Whitted-style rays, progressive path tracing, textured PBR, and an SDL/ImGui viewer.

You feed it .gltf / .glb from the command line. It pulls scene-graph transforms, cameras, and punctual lights. Shading is Lambert diffuse and Cook-Torrance GGX. PBR textures: base color, metallic, roughness, emissive, occlusion, normal.

gltF extensions in use: KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_lights_punctual. Simple transmission plus IOR gets a conservative glass mapping. Iridescence is a softened tinted preview. True thin-film comes later. Incomplete meshes get fallback normals and tangents. First-person camera, screenshot on P. BVH: a top-level object tree with diagnostics and optional refit, and a per-mesh triangle BVH, median split on the longest centroid axis. There's a built-in material lineup for glass, smooth metal, rough metal, and dielectric PBR. You can dump a PNG without the viewer, with async CPU progress and Ctrl+C to cancel. Optional IBL from LDR/HDR equirect maps.

Whitted path: recursive reflection and refraction, PBR local lights with hard and transparent shadows, textures and normal maps.

Path tracer: BRDF importance sampling, next event estimation, Russian roulette, low-discrepancy samples, emissive materials, temporal accumulation, a small SVGF-style preview denoiser with history reprojection. Tiled CPU rendering, progress, cancelable exports. Light picking: uniform, power, or contribution-weighted per shading point. Optional Intel Open Image Denoise if you build with ASTRATRACE_ENABLE_OIDN=ON.

Backends: cpu-whitted (default) and cpu-path. Samplers: random, Halton, Sobol.

C++20, CMake, SDL3, GLM, tinygltf, nlohmann/json, stb, OpenMP, optional OIDN.

projects.title: Parallel Deferred Renderer
projects.shortDescription: OpenGL 3.3 deferred renderer with a gRPC layer on top: replicas, failover, metrics, optional Spark streaming.
projects.fullDescription:
OpenGL deferred renderer. Geometry is one pass, lighting is another, so lots of lights don't wreck you. Phase 3 wraps that renderer in a gRPC service and treats it like a small fault-tolerant system.

G-buffer (position, normal, albedo) in the geometry pass, then lighting, SAO, post, forward, GUI. The G-buffer also keeps roughness, metalness, AO, depth, and velocity. Keys 1-9 flip debug views. BRDF is GGX, Smith, Schlick Fresnel, Disney diffuse. Point lights plus a directional, quadratic or UE4 attenuation. IBL from lat-long to cubemap, irradiance, prefiltered specular, BRDF LUT. Assimp for models (sphere, teapot, shader ball, OBJ, FBX, others). PBR materials: rusted iron, gold, wood floor. SAO, FXAA, motion blur, Reinhard / Filmic / Uncharted tonemap. Exposure from aperture, shutter, ISO. WASD camera, mouse look, ImGui, timings per pass. Code is split into camera, lighting, mesh, renderer, resources.

gRPC in front of the C++ OpenGL renderer. Two or more replicas, primary and standby, on 50051, 50052, and up. Client retries and fails over. Replica manager health-checks and restarts. Load generator with a rate and duration, including fake camera movement. Metrics: throughput, latency (P50 / P95 / P99), success rate, recovery time. Optional Spark streaming, micro-batches around 30 FPS.

From the README, a 120-second run: 3,438 requests, 99.21% success, 28.5 ms average latency, P50 26.3 ms, P95 45.2 ms, P99 68.7 ms, 28.6 req/s, 30 ms recovery. Streaming: 29.3 FPS, 1.4 ms frame latency, batches of 10 frames.

C++, OpenGL 3.3+, GLFW, GLAD, GLM, Assimp, STB, ImGui, CMake. Python 3.10+, gRPC, Spark if you want it.

projects.title: Interactive VR Architecture Showcase
projects.shortDescription: Commercial VR ArcViz. Walk interiors and exteriors in VR or first person, poke at furniture, materials, models. Sign-in from the menu to a Flask + Postgres backend. A 3ds Max plugin plus Datasmith/Dataprep builds the Unreal setup.
projects.fullDescription:
Commercial VR architecture visualization. VR if you have it, first person if you don't. You walk interiors and exteriors, swap furniture, materials, and models, take screenshots, change time of day, measure (and switch units), and pick a movement mode that's easier to use. TVs, lights, and doors respond.

Setup is automated. In 3ds Max, a designer uses a plugin I built: UI on the object or class for whether it's interactable and what the options are. That metadata gets baked on export through Datasmith. Unreal pulls the scene in with a Dataprep recipe and drops in the right interactive classes from what the designer set.

New levels can go out as pack files and mount at runtime, so you don't rebuild the whole project every time.

Users sign in from the main menu over HTTP. Backend is Python Flask and Postgres. Each account has levels and a subscription cap. They can request edits. There's an admin page to manage people and upload new packs. Users download those from there.

projects.title: Virtual Reality Training Simulation
projects.shortDescription: VR anatomy practice for medical students in Unreal. Hands only. Tracking, gestures, poses. Controllers stay out of it.
projects.fullDescription:
VR training for medical students, in Unreal. You can study anatomy in 3D without needing the physical lab for every pass.

The whole thing was built around hand tracking, gestures, and poses. Controllers stay out of it. That's how the immersion holds.

Detailed anatomical models, learning modules, feedback while you interact, progress and assessment, and multi-user support.

It's for repeating hard structures and tasks that don't scale well with plastic models and lab time.

projects.title: Real-Time AI Avatars
projects.shortDescription: Conversational MetaHumans I built for MarsX AI Solutions in the UAE. Backend talks to cloud or local LLMs, TTS (ElevenLabs through my Unreal plugin, or local like Chatterbox), STT, and Audio2Face, all from a character dashboard.
projects.fullDescription:
I built a MetaHuman you can talk to for MarsX AI Solutions in the UAE. It listens, thinks, answers out loud, and the face and body follow the voice. Nobody is puppeteering it.

Speech-to-text first. A backend I wrote sends that to an LLM (API or a model on the machine) with that character's background and knowledge. The reply goes to TTS. Cloud voices: ElevenLabs, through an Unreal plugin I made. Local voices: open-source TTS in-engine, Chatterbox and others in the same slot. That audio drives NVIDIA Audio2Face so the MetaHuman lipsyncs and emotes as it talks. Procedural animation keeps the body in a conversation. Different voices and knowledge per character.

The backend is the switchboard. Same MetaHuman, cloud LLM one day, local the next, no rebuild. ElevenLabs for production streaming TTS (and STT on that path). Local TTS/LLM when it has to stay on-prem. Audio2Face is live from the speech, a canned clip never enters that path.

Characters aren't baked into the level. A dashboard creates them, binds an ID the Unreal client loads, and gives each one background, lighting, voice, API settings, files, and knowledge. Stand up a new ambassador, point it at the right models and docs, and the runtime picks it up.

MarsX aims this at governments, exhibitions, museums, and enterprise work in the UAE, Arabic and English. The still is a MetaHuman from that line. No public repo.

projects.title: 3D Game Portfolio
projects.shortDescription: I made an Unreal-looking 3D portfolio you can walk around, plus a normal webpage, both on one Sanity CMS. The 3D ate the projects. So now it's a project.
projects.fullDescription:
This was my 3D gamified portfolio. Greybox, grid floor, viewport chrome, third-person movement, statues as portals. Unreal-flavored on purpose. It was too loud. People didn't look at the work. So it became a piece in this site.

Two fronts, one Sanity source. Game Mode is the 3D walkthrough. Normal Mode is a regular page with real headings and sections if you don't want the 3D, with a way back into Game Mode.

Game Mode is Three.js through React Three Fiber, Rapier physics, Drei controls. Third-person: WASD / arrows, Shift to sprint, drag to look. On a phone, a stick and look-touch. Kinematic capsule, grounded raycast, gravity, camera that raycasts so it doesn't clip walls. Top bar like a sim: ACTIVE_STATE, TERMINATE (quit to Normal Mode), REBOOT_ENTITY (respawn), FPS, mute. Loading screen, onboarding, PC and mobile tutorials. Statues for sections, labels when you're close, click to frame them, HTML overlays for the content, a quest modal and toasts for poking around. Quality tiers, an adaptive monitor, an extreme FPS mode, reduced motion, optional sound.

Normal Mode has the same projects, education, work, skills, contact, about, and blog. Sanity Studio for settings, sections, media, timelines, skills, the character GLB/animations/speeds, and the scene primitives. It was on Cloudflare Pages.

React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, postprocessing, Sanity, Tailwind, Zustand, Framer Motion.

projects.title: Quizify
projects.shortDescription: ASP.NET learning site. Quizzes, some social bits, a bit of gamification, running on Azure.
projects.fullDescription:
Quizify is a learning site I built with ASP.NET Razor Pages and C#. You can write quizzes, there's a social layer, and it tracks progress.

Razor Pages on the server, SQL for content and users, Azure App Services, CI/CD through Azure DevOps, accounts with auth.

You can create and manage quizzes, do the social learning flow, see progress, and there's a gamified loop for feedback.

We documented it, tested it, and shipped it in passes.

projects.title: Blackmagic Camera Control Center
projects.shortDescription: Desktop app I wrote so I can run the Blackmagic Camera iOS app from a computer. REST and WebSockets, their documented API. I don't have to touch the phone.
projects.fullDescription:
I got tired of poking the phone while shooting, so I wrote Blackmagic Camera Control Center. It remotes the Blackmagic Camera app on iOS, or anything speaking that Camera Control REST API. Record, expose, run the set from a desktop. Package version 0.1.0.

The phone already exposes recording, exposure, lens, audio, overlays, slate, presets, media, color, livestream, and telemetry on the LAN. The phone UI is awkward when you're filming. This turns that API into dockable panels, live status, and keyboard control.

It's an npm workspaces monorepo. packages/shared holds TypeScript types, the endpoint registry, WebSocket protocols, and state diffs. packages/server is Fastify, undici, ws, bonjour-service. packages/web is React 18, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn-style UI, zustand, dockview, sonner. The browser never talks to cameras. Self-signed TLS and mDNS are hostile in a browser, so the path is camera to HTTPS REST and a camera WebSocket (TLS on the LAN) to the server, then /api REST proxy and /api/stream WebSocket to the web app.

Cameras show up via mDNS (_blackmagic._tcp) or you type an IP. iOS control is usually HTTPS 4444. Hardware boxes get probed on 4444, 443, and 80. Each camera is isolated so one dropout doesn't kill the rest. Reconnect backs off from 2s to 30s. On connect, a REST sweep fills state, then the camera's event WebSocket keeps it live. Writes the camera doesn't event (record, livestream, autofocus, auto WB, slate reset, presets, media) get re-read after the call. RTT is shown as connection quality. The backend loads that camera's OpenAPI docs and greys out controls it doesn't have, ND on an iPhone for example. 404/501 can mark paths unsupported at runtime. A transparent REST proxy forwards any camera path, including stuff added in later app versions, without a backend change.

Panels: Cameras, Multi View (grid with tally, timecode, storage, battery, quick REC, 1-9 picks the active camera), Recording (status, stop asks first), then Exposure, Lens, Audio, Color, Monitoring, Slate, Media, Presets, Stream. Events plus toasts for recording, storage/battery bands, and connection. Workspaces save dock layouts. The current one autosaves. Dark-first, light theme if you want. Shortcuts: R record (stop is guarded), 1-9 camera, F fullscreen, T theme, ? help.

Exposure: ISO, shutter speed/angle, auto exposure, white balance and tint, auto WB, ND, gain, sharpening. Lens: focus, autofocus, zoom, iris, OIS, per-device labels. Audio: per-channel input, gain, phantom, pad, low-cut. Color: lift, gamma, gain, offset, contrast, hue/sat, luma contribution. Monitoring: zebra, focus assist, false color, frame guides, grids, safe area, LUT, clean feed. Slate: scene/take/shot/reel/lens/project, increment and reset. Media: working set, active media, format with a guard. Presets: list, apply, save, delete. Livestream: platform, start/stop. Persistence is JSON (cameras, workspaces, preferences).

There's a mock camera for development and Vitest: ticking timecode, storage that drains, battery that dies. Node 20+.

The REST API has no video feed and no audio meters. You see gain. Preset binary download isn't proxied. Apply, save, and delete work. Some properties (livestream status) are polled. v1.1 is sketched as MediaMTX SRT/RTMP ingest and WebRTC preview in the tiles. Still a stub.

Cloud accounts, a mobile client, and pulling files off the camera never made it in.

projects.title: Haze Launcher
projects.shortDescription: OOAD course work. Design only. User stories, PlantUML, Figma. A Steam-like launcher: library, store, news, clans, friends.
projects.fullDescription:
Haze Launcher is a design project from an object-oriented analysis and design course. Design only. I wrote the user stories and the design for a Steam-like launcher with a modern UI: library, store, news, clans, friends. Social stuff on top of buying and running games.

The spec starts from a split life. Store here, library there, achievements somewhere else. Haze is specified as one place for that.

SRS use cases, fully dressed (actors, main flow, alternatives, pre/post): register, login, browse, buy, friends, achievements. Browse is catalog, search/filter, details. Purchase is payment and into the library. Friends is search, request, accept/reject. Achievements per game from the library. Non-functional notes in the spec: persisted data, 50 concurrent users at 3s or under, encryption for sensitive data, 99.9% availability.

Domain: User, Library, Game, Achievement, Friend, Payment, Email. A user owns a library, has many-to-many friends, earns achievements on games, payments send a confirmation email. Class design adds register/login/browse/purchase/friends/achievements, library add/remove, payment process/verify. ER diagram for persistence. OCL in the SDS: unique email, password rules, enough funds, bidirectional friendship, a friend cap, unique games in a library, achievements only on owned games.

On paper the SDS splits user management, store, library, achievements, social. Four layers: presentation, application, domain, persistence. Intended mapping: Java, Spring Boot, Thymeleaf, MySQL, Spring Data JPA, JWT, BCrypt. Patterns called out: Singleton (config), Factory (payments), Observer (library/update notifications).

Diagrams are PlantUML: use cases, domain, class, ERD, logical architecture, sequence (purchase, unlock achievement), interaction (login, purchase), activity (registration, purchase, achievements), state machines for UI (auth, library, achievements). Figma in the SDS: Home (featured, news, store, library), Login, Library, Game, News. The still is the Game Library screen from that file.

The GitHub repo has the SRS, SDS, PlantUML, exported PNGs, and the Figma assets.

projects.title: Python 2D Physics Engine
projects.shortDescription: 2D physics in Python, shown as an 8-ball pool game.
projects.fullDescription:
A 2D physics engine in Python, demoed as 8-ball pool in Pygame. Position-based dynamics, Verlet integration, iterative constraints.

Bodies have mass, inertia, restitution. Verlet keeps the timestep stable. A position-based solver handles soft and rigid contacts.

Collisions: circle-circle and circle-edge, impulses plus a penetration fix. Distance constraints for springy stuff. Friction through contact forces.

In the pool game you can tweak ball mass, friction, and restitution, aim the cue with angle and power, pocket balls, reset the table.

Python 3.8+, Pygame, NumPy. Physics is a separate module from the table.

projects.title: PathFinder-AI
projects.shortDescription: Python grid pathfinding visualizer. A handful of search algorithms, and you can watch them run.
projects.fullDescription:
PathFinder-AI is a Python visualizer for pathfinding on a grid. An agent walks an n by n map with obstacles, pickups, and a goal, trying to grab items along the way while you watch the search unfold in Pygame.

State is position plus what you've collected. Four-way movement, no diagonals.

Uninformed: DFS, BFS, iterative deepening. Informed: greedy best-first and A*. Cost: uniform cost. Local: hill climbing and simulated annealing.

Grid and state are objects. NetworkX and Matplotlib draw the search tree. Tests cover valid paths, optimality, and a few nasty layouts.

Search code is separate from the view, so adding an algorithm or a map isn't a rewrite.

projects.title: Eleven Labs Unreal Engine Plugin
projects.shortDescription: Unreal runtime plugin for ElevenLabs streaming TTS. Blueprint-first, async, PCM packaged as WAV, helpers to play it.
projects.fullDescription:
A runtime Unreal plugin for ElevenLabs streaming text-to-speech. Blueprint-first. Async APIs, PCM packed into WAV, helpers to play audio at runtime. The .uplugin says 0.1.0 (beta). Category: Audio.

There's a runtime module ElevenLabs (Type = Runtime, LoadingPhase = Default). Settings live under Edit, Project Settings, Plugins, Eleven Labs (API key, default timeout). UElevenLabsSynthesizeTextAsync is the Blueprint/C++ entry. HTTP streams ElevenLabs /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id}/stream. Optional per-chunk callbacks. A full WAV always comes back on success. Helpers: PCM16 to WAV, WAV to USoundWaveProcedural, optional save under Saved/ElevenLabs/*.wav.

Still missing, though the layout allows it: STT, voice listing, dubbing, history, auth beyond the plugin key, canceling in-flight requests, multi-channel. This path is mono.

You call SynthesizeTextToWav with text and FElevenLabsTTSConfig (voice ID required, default model eleven_multilingual_v2). It checks text, voice, and key, POSTs the stream, accumulates PCM (keeps an odd leftover byte), builds WAV. ChunkMode Progressive fires per-chunk WAV events. AssembleThenReturn waits for the whole line. Success: OnReceive with bIsFinal true. Failure: OnError (empty text, missing voice, missing key, HTTP/timeout, empty audio, WAV packaging).

Audio: pcm at the requested rate (default 16000, min 8000), 16-bit, mono. Playback is USoundWaveProcedural in SOUNDGROUP_Voice.

Build depends on Core, CoreUObject, Engine, HTTP, Json, JsonUtilities, DeveloperSettings.

projects.title: 3DS Max Automation Plugin
projects.shortDescription: Version-agnostic 3ds Max C++ plugin from the VR architecture showcase. Designers set metadata in Max. Datasmith and Dataprep finish the Unreal setup.
projects.fullDescription:
This is the 3ds Max plugin from Interactive VR Architecture Showcase. C++ SDK, not tied to one Max version. It runs on most recent ones.

A designer drops a modifier on the object. That's the UI for metadata: what this thing should be in Unreal, and the interaction options, other models to swap, materials on parts of the mesh. The plugin writes it onto the object so Datasmith carries it. In Unreal, a Dataprep recipe reads it and applies the matching interactive setup.

UI in Max, data on the object, Datasmith out, Dataprep in Unreal. Scene ready without wiring every asset by hand.

projects.title: Me vs. Darth Vader

projects.fullDescription:
Eight seconds of a fight in Unreal Engine 5.5. A MetaHuman with my face, Darth Vader, a battle around them.

projects.fullDescription:

projects.title: MetaHuman Self-Portrait
projects.shortDescription: A MetaHuman of me that I rebuild when the tools get better. Latest is an iPhone face scan in Unreal 5.8, body and accessories matched, dropped into the Game Animation Sample.
projects.fullDescription:
This is a MetaHuman of me. I redo it when new MetaHuman tools land. This version is the closest so far on body, accessories, face, and hair.

Face came from an iPhone scan in Polycam, cleaned in Blender, then imported into Unreal Engine 5.8 as a MetaHuman identity, with Creator handling fat, muscle, height, per-part height, and the rest of the body sliders.

Accessories match what I wear: glasses, ring, bracelet, Apple Watch. I modeled the glasses and the ring. Glasses got textures and materials in the Unreal shader graph. Hair is Creator hair at the same length.

An animation blueprint runs procedural face stuff. The character lives in Unreal's Game Animation Sample. The video is me walking him around in that project. Stills: a close-up, and the same shot with DLSS 5.
